Oral Health 
Interoperability 
Alliance 
Better Care Through Connected 
Health Information 
 
 
 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Attention: CMS–0062–P 
P.O. Box 8013, Baltimore, MD 21244-8013. 
Re: CMS–0062–P —Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, 
Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) 
Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
Facilitated Exchanges 
Dear Dr. Oz: 
The Oral Health Interoperability Alliance (OHIA) commends CMS’s continued leadership in advancing 
standards-based, interoperable infrastructure to improve access, transparency, and administrative 
efficiency across the U.S. health care system and appreciates the opportunity to comment on CMS-
0062-P. 
OHIA is a bipartisan, multi-stakeholder coalition committed to making oral health data a first-class part 
of the national interoperability ecosystem. Our participants include dental practice management and 
electronic dental record vendors, imaging and AI developers, clearinghouses, revenue cycle platforms, 
HIEs, QHINs, payers, public health agencies, standards experts, and patient advocates. OHIA members 
are actively engaged in HL7® standards development, implementation guide testing, and real-world 
implementation. 
Because dentistry remains unevenly represented in federal interoperability policy, CMS–0062–P 
presents an important opportunity to ensure that oral health is explicitly included in the next phase of 
standards-based prior authorization and API adoption. 
OHIA operates as a neutral convening forum focused on implementation-ready solutions. Our work is 
grounded in open, consensus-based standards and in practical alignment with federal policy levers. The 
recommendations reflected in this letter represent consensus-based positions developed through 
OHIA’s multi-stakeholder process, though they do not necessarily reflect unanimous agreement across 
all participants. OHIA members — including dental practice management vendors, clearinghouses, and 
payers — are active participants in Health Level Seven International (HL7®) activities including active 
testing and implementation guide development. 
Executive Summary 
OHIA supports CMS’s proposed direction in CMS–0062–P to advance interoperable, standards-based 
prior authorization and related application programming interface (API) capabilities. We encourage 
CMS to explicitly and intentionally include dentistry throughout the final rule and related guidance 
so that dental plans, providers, vendors, and implementation partners are clearly within scope. With 
explicit inclusion, we also request that CMS establish dental-specific timelines where needed in 
order to enable individual dentists and dental service offices adequate time to prepare for this 
change. OHIA members are actively advancing standards-based alignment through implementation 
 Oral Health Interoperability Alliance  
Response to CMS-0062 
 6/15/2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Oral Health Interoperability Alliance 2 
 
guide development, testing, and real-world adoption. We are confident the oral health sector can 
still move aggressively toward a unified interoperability framework that better supports whole-
person health. 
Specifically, OHIA requests that CMS and HHS: 
1. Explicitly confirm in the final rule and accompanying guidance that dental payers, dental providers, 
dental practice management systems, and stand-alone dental plans are within the interoperability 
and prior authorization modernization framework. 
2. Establish a defined implementation pathway for stand-alone dental plans, including a three-year 
transition period where appropriate. 
3. Recognize dental prescribing workflows in drug prior authorization guidance, including use of RTPBC 
for real-time benefit classification before prior authorization is initiated. 
4. Ensure payer API conformance testing and ONC certification pathways include dental-specific code 
sets, workflows, attachments, and prior authorization scenarios. 
5. Adopt a flexible versioning pathway and specific timeline for CRD, DTR, PAS, CDex, and oral-health-
related FHIR implementation guides so dental implementers are not required to build to outdated 
specifications. 
6. Begin a defined transition away from Direct Data Entry (DDE) portals, adopting standards-based 
electronic workflows, with timelines calibrated to dental market readiness. 
OHIA offers these comments in the spirit of partnership and stands ready to support CMS and ONC 
with technical input, implementation resources, testing insights, and dental use cases that can help 
accelerate this transition. The detailed recommendations below explain how removing ambiguity for 
dental stakeholders, paired with implementation timelines calibrated to the dental market, can 
advance CMS’s goals while accelerating progress toward whole-person health. 
 
I. Stand-Alone Dental Plans (Section I.C Solicitation) 
CMS solicits comment on whether future rulemaking should bring stand-alone dental plans (SADPs) into 
the full CMS interoperability application programming interface (API) requirements. OHIA encourages 
CMS to include SADPs in the interoperability ecosystem and to do so in a way that recognizes the 
progress already underway across the market. Many payers, including those that offer SADPs on the 
federal and state-based exchanges, are actively working toward interoperable capabilities based on Fast 
Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. To support smaller plans and promote durable 
implementation, OHIA encourages CMS to provide a three-year transition window that gives all SADPs a 
realistic path into the broader interoperability framework while maintaining overall market progress. 
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) proposals partially close this gap 
— SADPs will be required to implement FHIR-based prior authorization (PA) under HIPAA — but they 
remain exempt from Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs. HIPAA compliance alone 
does not deliver the interoperability architecture that makes PA data clinically useful. As medical payers 
implement the full API suite, SADPs operating on legacy portal workflows create a structural break in 
care coordination at exactly the point where oral-systemic data exchange matters most. 
 Oral Health Interoperability Alliance  
Response to CMS-0062 
 6/15/2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Oral Health Interoperability Alliance 3 
 
II. Drug Prior Authorization and the Dental Prescribing Question (Sections 
I.C / II.B) 
OHIA strongly supports CMS’s proposal to extend electronic prior authorization (ePA) to drugs and 
encourages CMS to recognize the Consumer Real-Time Pharmacy Benefit Check (RTPBC) 
Implementation Guide (IG) Version 2.0 as the appropriate mechanism for benefit classification queries—
particularly in dentistry, where existing NCPDP-based workflows are not yet deeply embedded. RTPBC is 
designed to return real-time information on drug coverage and benefit classification, identifying which 
benefit covers a given drug for a specific patient under a specific plan before any prior authorization 
transaction is initiated. The Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD) then follows that 
determination and assumes benefit classification is already known. Using RTPBC at the point of 
prescribing, rather than relying on manual plan document review or portal navigation, reflects the 
correct workflow sequence and builds on an implementation guide already in active use and that has 
been harmonized with NCPDP’s Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) Standard Version 13. In dentistry, 
this also creates an opportunity to establish a more aggressive implementation timeline around the 
emerging standards-based approach rather than requiring migration from a mature legacy workflow. 
OHIA also encourages explicit inclusion of dental-specific drug categories in RTPBC implementation 
guidance so the standard works effectively across the full prescribing community. That clarity would 
help reduce avoidable implementation challenges, particularly for small and rural dental practices. 
 
III. Payer API Conformance and ONC Certification (Sections II.E / II.F) 
OHIA supports CMS recommending extension of ONC certification to payer-side API implementations 
and encourages any certification framework to include dental-specific testing tracks. OHIA and its 
members are prepared to help design, test, and validate those pathways by contributing dental use 
cases, workflow scenarios, implementation experience, and Connectathon-developed test data. That 
participation is important because current conformance approaches do not reliably detect several issues 
that are common in dental workflows, including inconsistent payer handling of Current Dental 
Terminology (CDT) codes, limited FHIR support in dental practice management systems, and the absence 
of dental-specific test scenarios. Recent revisions to dental sedation and anesthesia CDT codes have 
highlighted how quickly operational friction can emerge when dental-specific coding and workflow 
realities are not fully reflected in implementation expectations. Variation in payer adoption and 
documentation requirements has reinforced that challenge. Similar issues arise more broadly when 
dental code sets, attachments, treatment sequencing, or benefit determination logic are handled 
inconsistently across plans. A more complete certification approach would evaluate whether payer APIs 
can correctly process dental code sets, support dental-specific prior authorization scenarios, and return 
responses that are usable in actual dental practice settings. OHIA welcomes the opportunity to serve as 
an active implementation partner in that effort and to help ensure dental adoption moves forward as an 
integral part of the broader interoperability ecosystem. 
 Oral Health Interoperability Alliance  
Response to CMS-0062 
 6/15/2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Oral Health Interoperability Alliance 4 
 
IV. HIPAA Administrative Simplification: FHIR-Based Prior Authorization 
Standards (Section II.H) 
OHIA supports adoption of the Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation 
Templates and Rules (DTR), and Prior Authorization Support (PAS) implementation guides as the HIPAA 
standard for electronic prior authorization and stands ready to help test and advance dental 
implementation from the outset. We encourage CMS to explicitly name dentistry in the final rule and 
accompanying guidance and to establish a distinct implementation timeline for dental adoption where 
needed. That clarity is important because dental prior authorization workflows differ materially across 
the market: Medicaid dental programs often use the Accredited Standards Committee X12 278 
transaction, many commercial dental plans continue to rely on portals or other non-transactional 
processes, and pre-determination remains common for many dental services. 
For dentistry, the CRD–DTR–PAS sequence offers a practical improvement over current workflows. CRD 
can surface prior authorization requirements at the point of treatment planning, DTR can replace ad hoc 
documentation requests with computable questionnaires pre-populated from the clinical record, and 
PAS can replace asynchronous portal submissions with a more efficient transaction-based exchange. 
OHIA also encourages CMS to adopt the most current ballot-reconciled implementation guide versions 
at the time of final rulemaking and to establish a sub-regulatory process for future updates. The Oral 
Health Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) Implementation Guide is currently in active 
balloting with a January 2027 production target, and absent a more flexible update pathway, dental 
implementers may be required to build to guide versions that are outdated before the compliance date 
arrives. 
Finally, successful dental adoption will depend on explicit attention to several implementation issues in 
the final rule or accompanying guidance, including structured clinical data for DTR, radiographic 
attachments through Clinical Data Exchange (CDex), and support for the CDT code set in dental prior 
authorization transactions, including anesthesia and sedation-related scenarios. OHIA welcomes the 
opportunity to help test and refine these implementation pathways as part of broader interoperability 
adoption. 
V. Direct Data Entry Portal Exception (Section II.H RFI) 
OHIA supports the direction CMS describes and encourages HHS to initiate rulemaking to narrow and 
ultimately eliminate the DDE exception, with a transition timeline calibrated to dental sector readiness. 
OHIA and its members are prepared to help test practical alternatives that can reduce portal 
dependence across HIPAA administrative workflows. 
The portal is not a neutral convenience. It has allowed many dental administrative transactions to 
remain outside standardized electronic exchange for decades and imposes disproportionate burden on 
small practices that must navigate dozens of payer-specific environments. That burden is increasingly 
unnecessary as standards-based tools continue to mature. In addition to CRD for surfacing prior 
authorization requirements within clinical workflows, emerging approaches such as digital insurance 
cards, Secure, Modular, and Reusable Technology (SMART) Health Cards, and SMART Health Links create 
new opportunities to reduce repeated portal lookups, manual data entry, and payer-specific front-end 
processes. OHIA encourages CMS to treat this request for information (RFI) as the beginning of a defined 
transition strategy, not an indefinite inquiry. 
 Oral Health Interoperability Alliance  
Response to CMS-0062 
 6/15/2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Oral Health Interoperability Alliance 5 
 
VI. Requests for Information 
OHIA would like to offer the following recommendations for the formal Requests for 
Information (RFI) for expansion of electronic event notifications and step therapy.  
A. Electronic Event Notifications 
OHIA encourages CMS to explicitly include dental providers as eligible recipients in any future 
expansion of electronic event notification requirements. Dental providers coordinate care for 
patients with diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, head and neck cancer, and 
other conditions where oral health status, infection risk, medication use, and treatment timing are 
clinically relevant. 
OHIA also encourages CMS to treat ADT notifications as a transitional capability, not the endpoint 
for event notification policy. ADT-based notification is useful but too narrow to support the full 
range of oral-systemic care coordination needs. CMS should prioritize FHIR Subscriptions as the 
preferred long-term, standards-based approach because they can support broader, more targeted 
clinical event notifications through the same API-based interoperability framework CMS is advancing 
elsewhere in this rule. 
CMS should avoid locking event notification policy into an ADT-only model and should include 
dental-specific use cases in future guidance, testing, and certification activities related to FHIR-based 
event notification. 
B. Step Therapy 
OHIA also encourages CMS to address dental use cases in any future policy or guidance related to 
step therapy and prior authorization. Step therapy concepts can arise in dental benefit 
administration, including for implants, orthodontics, periodontal procedures, and other services 
where coverage may depend on prior treatment history, failed or completed alternative treatments, 
disease progression, benefit sequencing, or documentation of medical or dental necessity. 
For these workflows, access to prior dental benefit and treatment history is essential. OHIA 
recommends that CMS confirm that dental benefit history, prior authorization history, and related 
treatment information are within scope of Payer-to-Payer data exchange when relevant to 
coverage, care coordination, or continuity of treatment. This would help ensure that receiving 
payers can access information about prior treatment across plan years and coverage transitions, 
reducing duplicative documentation requests and avoiding unnecessary delays for patients and 
providers. 
OHIA further encourages CMS to clarify that dental payers should implement Payer-to-Payer 
exchange capabilities in a manner that supports dental-specific benefit sequencing, CDT code 
history, prior authorization determinations, and documentation relevant to step therapy-like 
requirements. Including these dental use cases in future guidance would help prevent dental 
workflows from remaining dependent on manual records requests, payer portals, or patient-
supplied documentation when standardized exchange can better support continuity of care. 
 
 Oral Health Interoperability Alliance  
Response to CMS-0062 
 6/15/2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Oral Health Interoperability Alliance 6 
 
Conclusion 
The proposed adoption of the Da Vinci FHIR implementation guides as the HIPAA standard for electronic 
prior authorization is the right policy direction. Dental payers and dental providers are HIPAA covered 
entities and should be expressly included in this framework so there is no ambiguity about scope, 
responsibility, or implementation expectations. Ensuring oral health is treated as part of whole-person 
health data exchange in the final rule and accompanying guidance would strengthen alignment across 
the health care system and better support whole-person health. Without explicit dental inclusion, the 
final rule risks creating a two-tier interoperability system in which medical prior authorization becomes 
increasingly automated while dental prior authorization remains dependent on payer portals, manual 
documentation, and inconsistent transaction workflows. 
At the same time, successful implementation will require recognition of the operational realities of the 
dental market. In selected areas, distinct implementation timelines may be needed to reflect differences 
in workflows, technical readiness, and current transaction patterns across Medicaid, commercial dental, 
and pre-determination environments. With that recognition, the oral health sector can move 
aggressively toward standards-based adoption and more fully participate in the broader interoperability 
ecosystem. 
OHIA offers these comments in the spirit of partnership. Our coalition is actively engaged in standards 
development, implementation guide testing, and real-world workflow design, and we stand ready to 
support CMS and ONC with dental-specific use cases, testing resources, and implementation expertise. 
OHIA welcomes the opportunity to meet with CMS and ONC staff to discuss these comments further 
and to help advance practical implementation pathways that ensure dentistry is fully and intentionally 
integrated into this next phase of interoperability policy. Taken together, these recommendations would 
improve prior authorization, modernize HIPAA administrative transactions, and reduce reliance on 
fragmented portal-based workflows. They would also help ensure that dentistry is fully integrated into 
the national interoperability framework rather than treated as a separate or secondary system.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Oral Health Interoperability Alliance (OHIA)
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Technology and standards coalition / Other
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** OHIA describes itself as a bipartisan, multi-stakeholder coalition including dental practice management and EDR vendors, imaging and AI developers, clearinghouses, revenue cycle platforms, HIEs, QHINs, payers, public health agencies, standards experts, and patient advocates. Members participate in HL7 standards development, IG testing, and real-world implementation.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

OHIA supports CMS's standards-based prior authorization and API direction but asks CMS to explicitly include dentistry and stand-alone dental plans in the interoperability framework. It recommends dental-specific implementation pathways, RTPBC use for dental prescribing benefit classification, dental testing in payer API/ONC certification, flexible FHIR versioning, attention to CDT/CDex/radiographic attachments, and a transition away from DDE portals calibrated to dental market readiness.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS/stand-alone dental plan RFI; GENERAL/RFIs.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** References CMS-0062-P sections I.C, II.B, II.E, II.F, II.H, and RFIs; no specific CFR citations emphasized.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; HL7; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, PAS; CDex; Consumer Real-Time Pharmacy Benefit Check (RTPBC) IG v2.0; NCPDP RTPB Standard v13; CDT code set; FHIR Subscriptions; SMART Health Cards; SMART Health Links; DDE; X12 278; Oral Health FHIR Implementation Guide.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Explicit inclusion of dentistry**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** Dentistry is unevenly represented in federal interoperability policy, and ambiguity could leave dental PA dependent on portals and manual workflows.
- **Specific request:** Explicitly confirm that dental payers, dental providers, dental practice management systems, and stand-alone dental plans are within the interoperability and PA modernization framework.

**Topic 2: Stand-alone dental plans**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** SADPs remain exempt from Patient Access, Provider Access, and Payer-to-Payer APIs even though HIPAA FHIR-based PA proposals partially close the gap.
- **Specific request:** Include SADPs in the interoperability ecosystem with a defined implementation pathway and a three-year transition period where appropriate.

**Topic 3: Dental prescribing and RTPBC**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Dental workflows may not have mature NCPDP-based infrastructure, and benefit classification should occur before PA initiation.
- **Specific request:** Recognize Consumer RTPBC IG v2.0 as the mechanism for benefit classification queries and include dental-specific drug categories in RTPBC implementation guidance.

**Topic 4: Payer API conformance and ONC certification**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Current conformance approaches do not reliably detect dental workflow issues such as CDT handling, dental attachments, and dental PA scenarios.
- **Specific request:** Include dental-specific code sets, workflows, attachments, treatment sequencing, and prior authorization scenarios in payer API conformance testing and ONC certification pathways.

**Topic 5: HIPAA FHIR-based PA adoption**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** OHIA supports adoption of CRD, DTR, and PAS as the HIPAA PA standard but notes dental workflows vary across Medicaid, commercial dental, portal, and pre-determination environments.
- **Specific request:** Explicitly name dentistry in final rule/guidance, establish a distinct dental timeline where needed, and include structured clinical data, radiographic attachments through CDex, and CDT support.

**Topic 6: Versioning and oral health IG pathway**
- **Provision ID:** ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Dental implementers could be forced to build to outdated specifications if final rules lock fixed versions while oral health IG work continues.
- **Specific request:** Adopt current ballot-reconciled IG versions at final rulemaking and establish a sub-regulatory update process, including for CRD, DTR, PAS, CDex, and oral-health-related FHIR IGs.

**Topic 7: DDE portal exception**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; EXISTING-WORKFLOWS
- **Position:** Modify / Support transition away
- **Rationale:** Portals perpetuate payer-specific workflows and disproportionately burden small dental practices.
- **Specific request:** Initiate rulemaking to narrow and ultimately eliminate the DDE exception with a readiness-calibrated transition timeline.

**Topic 8: Event notifications and step therapy dental use cases**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Dental providers need access to broader care coordination information and step therapy-like dental benefit history.
- **Specific request:** Include dental providers as eligible recipients for event notifications; treat FHIR Subscriptions as the long-term approach; include dental benefit history, prior authorization history, CDT history, and documentation in Payer-to-Payer exchange.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S2/S3:** OHIA supports required FHIR IG adoption but asks for flexible versioning and sub-regulatory updates so dental implementers use current specifications.
- **S8/S9:** OHIA references SMART Health Cards, SMART Health Links, and FHIR Subscriptions as tools to reduce portal lookups and support event notifications.
- **S12/S15:** OHIA addresses dental prescribing and benefit classification, recommending RTPBC before PA initiation.
- **S23/S24/S26/S33:** OHIA supports payer API conformance/certification that includes dental code sets, attachments, and scenarios.
- **S44-S56:** OHIA supports CRD/DTR/PAS as HIPAA electronic PA standards and asks CMS/HHS to explicitly include dentistry, with dental-specific implementation timelines where needed.
- **S60-S65:** OHIA supports updated standards and flexible version pathways for oral health-related FHIR IGs.
- **S66-S82:** OHIA responds to RFIs on event notifications, DDE portals, and step therapy by requesting dental-specific use cases and Payer-to-Payer support.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Confirm dental payers, providers, practice management systems, and stand-alone dental plans are in scope.
2. Establish a defined SADP implementation pathway with a three-year transition period where appropriate.
3. Recognize RTPBC IG v2.0 for benefit classification before PA initiation in dental prescribing workflows.
4. Include dental-specific drug categories in RTPBC implementation guidance.
5. Include CDT codes, dental workflows, attachments, and dental PA scenarios in payer API conformance testing and ONC certification.
6. Adopt CRD, DTR, and PAS as HIPAA PA standards while explicitly naming dentistry.
7. Use current ballot-reconciled IG versions and create a flexible sub-regulatory update pathway.
8. Address structured clinical data, radiographic attachments through CDex, and CDT support.
9. Narrow and ultimately eliminate the DDE exception through readiness-calibrated rulemaking.
10. Include dental providers in event notification policy and support FHIR Subscriptions as the long-term model.
11. Confirm dental benefit history and PA history are in scope for Payer-to-Payer exchange.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Ambiguity about dental inclusion, two-tier interoperability, outdated standards, insufficient dental conformance testing, ongoing portal dependence, and lack of dental-specific data exchange.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Dental PA may remain manual while medical PA becomes automated; small and rural dental practices may face avoidable burden; oral-systemic care coordination may suffer.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Dental market readiness, limited FHIR support in dental practice management systems, inconsistent CDT handling, attachments/radiographs, legacy portal workflows, pre-determination practices.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No numeric statistics cited.
- **Studies or research referenced:** No external studies cited; comment relies on coalition expertise, HL7 participation, Connectathon-developed test data, and real-world implementation experience.
- **Examples provided:** Dental sedation/anesthesia CDT code revisions; dental radiographic attachments; implants, orthodontics, periodontal procedures, and step therapy-like benefit sequencing.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Dental payers, SADPs, dentists, DSOs, dental vendors, clearinghouses, payers, patients, ONC, CMS, HL7 participants.
- **Economic implications:** Portal dependence and payer-specific processes impose burden, especially on small practices; calibrated timelines could reduce implementation shock.
- **Technical feasibility:** OHIA believes standards-based dental adoption is feasible with explicit scope, testing, version flexibility, and dental-specific use cases.
- **Patient care impact:** Better dental interoperability can improve whole-person care coordination, reduce PA delays, and preserve continuity across dental/medical workflows.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with scope and implementation modifications
- **Tone:** Technical, collaborative, implementation-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We encourage CMS to explicitly and intentionally include dentistry throughout the final rule and related guidance" - Context: Executive summary scope request.
2. "HIPAA compliance alone does not deliver the interoperability architecture that makes PA data clinically useful." - Context: SADP/API framework argument.
3. "The proposed adoption of the Da Vinci FHIR implementation guides as the HIPAA standard for electronic prior authorization is the right policy direction." - Context: HIPAA PA standards support.
4. "The portal is not a neutral convenience." - Context: DDE portal exception critique.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests dental-specific timelines and three-year SADP transition where appropriate.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Notes burden on small/rural dental practices and market readiness issues.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Strong focus on reducing portal and manual documentation burden for dentists.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not a central focus.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Whole-person oral-systemic care and small/rural dental practice concerns are relevant.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Extensive discussion of dental API, FHIR, CDex, CDT, RTPBC, and conformance testing.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Central focus on IG versions, oral health IG, and sub-regulatory updates.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Better dental PA workflows can reduce delays and support continuity.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not directly challenged.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Offers coalition support and Connectathon/test data participation.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Addresses benefit classification and dental prescribing.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests clear scope and guidance so dental stakeholders know obligations.
- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Addresses SADPs and smaller plans/practices.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Discusses portals, pre-determination, X12, and dental workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Dental vendors, clearinghouses, practice management systems, and certification are central.
